questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A light spring of natural length 10.0 cm is attached to the floor of a container. A mass is placed on top of the spring.

When the container is lifted upwards at a constant speed, the length of the spring is 7.5 cm. The container then moves upwards with a constant deceleration of 2.0 m $\mathrm{s}^{-2}$.

What is the new length of the spring?
questions.stemText: A light spring of natural length 10.0 cm is attached to the floor of a container. A mass is placed on top of the spring. When the container is lifted upwards at a constant speed, the length of the spring is 7.5 cm. The container then moves upwards with a constant deceleration of 2.0 m s−2. What is the new length of the spring? A 7.0 cm B 8.0 cm C 12.0 cm D 13.0 cm
questions.difficultyReason: Students must determine the acceleration direction and eliminate the spring constant using the initial compression.
questions.misconception: Treating upward motion as upward acceleration

explanation.body: At constant speed the compression is $x_1=10.0-7.5=2.5\ \mathrm{cm}$ and $mg=kx_1$. While the container slows, its acceleration is downward and $mg-kx_2=ma$. Substituting $mg=kx_1$ and dividing by $mg$ gives $a/g=(x_1-x_2)/x_1$, so $x_2=1.99\ \mathrm{cm}\approx2.0\ \mathrm{cm}$. The new length is $10.0-2.0=8.0\ \mathrm{cm}$.

perOption.A: Treats the acceleration as upward and increases the compression.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Adds the reduced compression to the natural length as though the spring were stretched.
perOption.D: Adds an increased compression to the natural length, reversing both the acceleration and the deformation.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A uniform beam of 10 kg is resting against a rough wall at an angle of 60° to it as shown in the figure below. It is attached to an inextensible string which is fixed to the wall at an angle of 30° to the vertical.

What is the tension T in the string?
questions.stemText: A uniform beam of 10 kg is resting against a rough wall at an angle of 60° to it as shown in the figure below. It is attached to an inextensible string which is fixed to the wall at an angle of 30° to the vertical. string 30° 60° beam wall What is the tension T in the string? A 85 N B 110 N C 130 N D 170 N
questions.difficultyReason: Students must determine the lever arms and opposing moments of both tension components and the beam’s weight.
questions.misconception: Using the full beam length for the weight’s lever arm

explanation.body: Take moments about the point where the beam contacts the wall. For beam length $L$ and weight $W$, the clockwise and anticlockwise moments balance when $(T\cos30^\circ)(L\sin60^\circ)=(T\sin30^\circ)(L\cos60^\circ)+\tfrac12W(L\sin60^\circ)$. With $W=(10)(9.81)\ \mathrm N$, this gives $T=85\ \mathrm N$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Balancing the vertical tension component against the full weight gives about $110\ \mathrm N$ and overlooks the wall’s friction.
perOption.C: This tension gives too large a clockwise moment after both tension components are included.
perOption.D: Uses the full horizontal span as the weight’s lever arm even though the weight acts at the midpoint.

questions.stemText:
Diagram 1 shows two forces $F$ acting on a circular disc of radius $r$. The disc is pivoted at a fixed point O which is the center of the disc. The forces give rise to a net moment $M$.

[Diagram 1. A downward force $F$ acts $r/2$ to the left of O, and an upward force $F$ acts $r/2$ to the right of O.]

In diagram 2, the lines of action of forces are moved to new points.

[Diagram 2. A downward force $F$ acts $3r/4$ to the left of O, and a horizontal force $F$ acts to the right, tangentially at the top of the disc.]

What is the net moment now?

Option — magnitude — direction
A — $M/4$ — anti-clockwise
B — $M/4$ — clockwise
C — $\frac{4}{3}M$ — anti-clockwise
D — $\frac{4}{3}M$ — clockwise

appearances.originalFile: grail:10416 ACJC 2023 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: Students must identify both moment arms and track the sense of each moment.
questions.misconception: Losing the sign of a moment.

explanation.body: In diagram 1 both moments are anticlockwise, so $M=2F(r/2)=Fr$. In diagram 2 the top force produces a clockwise moment $Fr$, and the left force produces an anticlockwise moment $3Fr/4$. The clockwise moment is larger, leaving a net moment of $Fr/4=M/4$ clockwise.

perOption.A: Reverses the sense of the larger moment.
perOption.B: Correct. The clockwise moment exceeds the anticlockwise moment by $M/4$.
perOption.C: Uses a ratio of moment arms for the magnitude and reverses the direction.
perOption.D: Uses a ratio of moment arms in place of subtracting the opposing moments.

questions.difficultyReason: Students must resolve three forces, find their resultant and reverse its direction.
questions.misconception: Reporting the resultant instead of the balancing force.

explanation.body: Taking right and up as positive, the resultant has components $R_x=40+50\sin45^\circ-70\sin72^\circ=8.78\ \mathrm{N}$ and $R_y=50\cos45^\circ+70\cos72^\circ=57.0\ \mathrm{N}$. The weight $W$ of the climber is $520\ \mathrm{N}$ and the reaction force $R$ acts at right angles to the wall. The climber is in equilibrium.

Which row shows the value of the tension $T$ in the rope and $R$?

$T/\mathrm{N}$ | $R/\mathrm{N}$
A 500 | 150
B 500 | 480
C 550 | 170
D 550 | 520

questions.misconception: Swapping the sine and cosine components.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A non-uniform rigid body is perfectly balanced on a smooth, fixed support.

Which of the following statements correctly describes the physical state of the body in this position?
questions.stemText: A non-uniform rigid body is perfectly balanced on a smooth, fixed support. Which of the following statements correctly describes the physical state of the body in this position? A The body is in equilibrium because the total mass on the left side of the support is exactly equal to the total mass on the right side of the support. B The support must be located at the geometric centre of the rigid body to ensure the resultant torque is zero. C The line of action of the body's weight passes directly through the support, ensuring the resultant torque is zero. D The body is in equilibrium because the upward force exerted by the body on the support is equal to the weight of the body.

options.label: A
options.text: The body is in equilibrium because the total mass on the left side of the support is exactly equal to the total mass on the right side of the support.

options.label: B
options.text: The support must be located at the geometric centre of the rigid body to ensure the resultant torque is zero.

options.label: C
options.text: The line of action of the body's weight passes directly through the support, ensuring the resultant torque is zero.

options.label: D
options.text: The body is in equilibrium because the upward force exerted by the body on the support is equal to the weight of the body.

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Qualitative application of centre of gravity and the zero-torque condition.
questions.misconception: Thinking balance requires equal mass on each side or a support at the geometric centre

explanation.body:
For equilibrium, the resultant torque about the support must be zero.

Since the body is balanced on a single support, the line of action of its weight must pass through the support.

perOption.A: Equal masses on each side do not give zero torque for a non-uniform body; moments depend on distances too.
perOption.B: For a non-uniform body the centre of gravity need not be at the geometric centre.
perOption.C: Correct. The weight then has zero moment about the support.
perOption.D: The force by the body on the support and the support's reaction are a Newton's third law pair acting on different bodies; they don't explain the body's equilibrium.

questions.stemText: A block of weight $W$ is suspended by two inextensible strings of equal length as shown. The strings are almost horizontal. [Diagram: two strings from a horizontal ceiling meet at a point just below the ceiling, each nearly horizontal; a short vertical string hangs from the junction to the block.] Which relationship between $W$ and the tension in one string $T$ is correct? A $T < \frac{W}{2}$ B $T = \frac{W}{2}$ C $\frac{W}{2} < T \le W$ D $T > W$

stemImage.alt: Question 3: A block of weight W is suspended by two inextensible strings of equal length as shown. The strings are almost horizontal. Which relationship between W and the t

appearances.originalFile: ACJC Physics/H2/2026 J2 H2 Physics Prelim P1 sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Requires resolving tensions vertically and reasoning about the small-angle limit.
questions.misconception: Assuming each string simply carries half the weight

explanation.body:
By symmetry, the tension $T$ in both strings is the same.

The vertical components balance the weight: $2T\sin\theta = W$, where $\theta$ is the small angle each string makes with the horizontal.

Since the strings are almost horizontal, $\sin\theta$ is very small, so $T = \dfrac{W}{2\sin\theta}$ must be greater than $W$.

perOption.A: $T$ can never be less than $W/2$; two strings must at least share the weight.
perOption.B: Only true if both strings were vertical.
perOption.C: Would need $\theta \ge 30^\circ$; nearly horizontal strings give much larger tension.
perOption.D: Correct. Small $\sin\theta$ makes $T \gg W$.

A student pulls a book from a shelf by its top corner, holding it between his forefinger and thumb. The book is uniform and has weight $W$ and dimensions $x$ and $y$ as shown.

[An upright book of horizontal width $x$ and vertical height $y$ is shown at the shelf edge, with a hand gripping its upper-right corner.]

What moment must the student provide at the corner of the book to stop it from rotating just before it leaves the shelf?

A $\frac{Wy}{2}$ anticlockwise
B $\frac{Wx}{2}$ anticlockwise
C $\frac{W(y-x)}{2}$ clockwise
D $Wx$ clockwise

questions.difficultyReason: The student must identify the shelf pivot and the perpendicular distance to the centre of gravity.
questions.misconception: Using the vertical dimension as the lever arm of a vertical force.

explanation.body: About the bottom-left corner of the book, its weight acts with horizontal lever arm $x/2$, producing a clockwise moment $Wx/2$. For rotational equilibrium the net moment about that corner is zero, so the student supplies an anticlockwise moment $Wx/2$.

perOption.A: Uses the vertical half-height as the lever arm of the vertical weight.
perOption.B: Correct.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
An air bubble in a tank of water is rising with constant velocity. The forces acting on the bubble are X, Y, and Z as shown.

Which of the following describes the three forces?
questions.stemText: An air bubble in a tank of water is rising with constant velocity. The forces acting on the bubble are X, Y, and Z as shown. Which of the following describes the three forces? A Z is the viscous drag on the bubble, Y is the weight of the bubble, X is the upthrust on the bubble and X = Y + Z. B Z is the viscous drag on the bubble, Y is the weight of the bubble, X is the upthrust on the bubble and X > Y + Z. C Z is the weight of the bubble, Y is viscous drag on the bubble, X is the upthrust on the bubble and X = Y + Z. D Z is the weight of the bubble, Y is viscous drag on the bubble, X is the upthrust on the bubble and X > Y + Z.

options.label: A
options.text: Z is the viscous drag on the bubble, Y is the weight of the bubble, X is the upthrust on the bubble and X = Y + Z.

options.label: B
options.text: Z is the viscous drag on the bubble, Y is the weight of the bubble, X is the upthrust on the bubble and X > Y + Z.

options.label: C
options.text: Z is the weight of the bubble, Y is viscous drag on the bubble, X is the upthrust on the bubble and X = Y + Z.

options.label: D
options.text: Z is the weight of the bubble, Y is viscous drag on the bubble, X is the upthrust on the bubble and X > Y + Z.

appearances.originalFile: grail:12935 2023 ASRJC H2 physics Promo P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student combines force directions and relative arrow lengths with the condition for constant velocity.
questions.misconception: Assuming upward motion requires a net upward force

explanation.body: Constant velocity means the forces balance, so $X=Y+Z$. The bubble’s weight is tiny, making it the shorter downward arrow $Y$. The upward force $X$ is upthrust, leaving the downward force $Z$ as viscous drag.

perOption.A: Correct. Upthrust balances the bubble’s weight and drag.
perOption.B: The inequality implies upward acceleration.
perOption.C: It assigns the bubble’s small weight to the larger downward arrow.
perOption.D: It swaps weight and drag and implies an upward resultant.

questions.stem:
A ladder is positioned on icy (frictionless) ground and is leant against a rough wall. At the instant of release it begins to slide.

Which diagram correctly shows the directions of the forces P, W and R acting on the ladder as it begins to slide?
questions.stemText: A ladder is positioned on icy (frictionless) ground and is leant against a rough wall. At the instant of release it begins to slide. Which diagram correctly shows the directions of the forces P, W and R acting on the ladder as it begins to slide? A P W B  C  D

appearances.originalFile: grail:12935 2023 ASRJC H2 physics Promo P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must combine the wall’s normal force and friction while keeping the ground reaction vertical.
questions.misconception: Adding a friction component at a frictionless contact

explanation.body: The frictionless ground exerts only a vertical upward normal force $R$. The weight $W$ acts vertically downwards. At the rough wall, upward friction and the horizontal normal force combine to give the upward-angled contact force $P$.

perOption.A: Weight should point vertically downwards.
perOption.B: Correct. The force directions match both contact surfaces and gravity.
perOption.C: The tilted ground reaction implies ground friction, and the horizontal wall force omits wall friction.
perOption.D: The tilted ground reaction implies friction at the icy ground.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
An object of weight $W$ is suspended from a newton meter. When the object is completely immersed in water, the newton meter reads $P$. When the object is completely immersed in oil, the newton meter reads $Q$.

[Two diagrams show the object suspended from a newton meter and fully submerged, first in water with reading $P$, then in oil with reading $Q$.]

What is the ratio $\frac{\text{density of oil}}{\text{density of water}}$?

A $\frac{W-P}{Q-P}$
B $\frac{Q-P}{W-P}$
C $\frac{W-P}{W-Q}$
D $\frac{W-Q}{W-P}$

stemImage.alt: Question 6: An object of weight W is suspended from a newton meter. When the object is completely immersed in water, the newton meter reads P. When the object is completely

appearances.originalFile: grail:14523 ASRJC 2024 JC2 H2 Physics Prelim P1

questions.difficultyReason: The student must write separate equilibrium equations and cancel the common displaced volume and gravitational field strength.
questions.misconception: Treating the difference between meter readings as an individual upthrust.

explanation.body: Taking upward as positive, equilibrium in water gives $P+V\rho_{\mathrm{water}}g-W=0$, so $\rho_{\mathrm{water}}=\frac{W-P}{Vg}$. In oil, $Q+V\rho_{\mathrm{oil}}g-W=0$, so $\rho_{\mathrm{oil}}=\frac{W-Q}{Vg}$. Dividing gives $\frac{\rho_{\mathrm{oil}}}{\rho_{\mathrm{water}}}=\frac{W-Q}{W-P}$.

perOption.A: Uses the water upthrust as the numerator and the difference in meter readings as the denominator.
perOption.B: Uses $Q-P$, the difference between the two upthrusts, as the oil upthrust.
perOption.C: Divides the water upthrust by the oil upthrust, giving the reciprocal.
perOption.D: Correct.

The portions A and B have masses of 20.0 kg and 30.0 kg respectively, and are of identical length, L.

What is the tension T in the cable?

B T A P 30o O 2L The portions A and B have masses of 20.0 kg and 30.0 kg respectively, and are of identical length, L. What is the tension T in the cable? A 150 N B 190 N C 230 N D 270 N

questions.difficultyReason: The student must infer the rod angle and find three perpendicular moment arms before balancing torques.
questions.misconception: Using along-rod distances as perpendicular moment arms

explanation.body: The rod is in equilibrium, so $\sum\tau=0$ about $O$. The triangle has equal sides $PO$ and the rod, both $2L$, so the rod is at $60^\circ$ to the horizontal. Taking moments about $O$ gives $T(2L\sin30^\circ)=20g(\frac{L}{2}\cos60^\circ)+30g(\frac{3L}{2}\cos60^\circ)$. Hence $T=269.78\ \mathrm{N}\approx270\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Underestimates the combined moment, giving a value close to the moment of B alone with its weight placed at the junction.
perOption.B: Using the junction as the point of action of B’s weight shortens its moment arm and gives about 196 N.
perOption.C: Omitting the moment from A gives about 221 N, close to this choice.
perOption.D: Correct. Both weights contribute to the moment about the pivot.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A fairground ride consists of four carriages connected to a vertical central pole, as shown in the following view from the top of the ride.

A motor rotates the central pole about its axis. This results in the four carriages each moving along a circular path.

The distance from the middle of each carriage to the centre of the pole is 3.20 m. When they are moving, each carriage experiences an air resistance force of 85.0 N. Assume that there are no other significant resistive forces.

Which torque does the motor need to apply to the pole to keep the system rotating at constant maximum speed?
questions.stemText: A fairground ride consists of four carriages connected to a vertical central pole, as shown in the following view from the top of the ride. A motor rotates the central pole about its axis. This results in the four carriages each moving along a circular path. The distance from the middle of each carriage to the centre of the pole is 3.20 m. When they are moving, each carriage experiences an air resistance force of 85.0 N. Assume that there are no other significant resistive forces. Which torque does the motor need to apply to the pole to keep the system rotating at constant maximum speed? A 5.44 N m B 272 N m C 544 N m D 1090 N m

appearances.originalFile: ASRJC/2026 H2 Physics Prelim P1 for sharing.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Sum of four equal moments for rotational equilibrium.
questions.misconception: Counting only one or two carriages

explanation.body: At constant speed, the motor torque balances the total torque from air resistance. Each of the four carriages experiences $85.0\ \mathrm{N}$ of air resistance at a radius of $3.20\ \mathrm{m}$. The required torque is $4(85.0)(3.20)=1088\ \mathrm{N\,m}\approx1090\ \mathrm{N\,m}$.

perOption.A: Grossly underestimates the torque from the four 85.0 N forces acting at a radius of 3.20 m.
perOption.B: Counts the torque from one carriage only.
perOption.C: Counts only two carriages, or one opposing pair.
perOption.D: Correct.

questions.stem: A wooden block of density 700 kg $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$ is completely submerged below the surface of water by a weight placed on top of it. The block floats to the surface when the weight is removed. The density of water is 1000 kg $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$.
questions.stemText: A wooden block of density 700 kg m-3 is completely submerged below the surface of water by a weight placed on top of it. The block floats to the surface when the weight is removed. The density of water is 1000 kg m-3. upthrust on the wooden block when it is completely submerged What is the ratio ? upthrust on the wooden block when it is floating A 0.143 B 0.700 C 1.43 D 7.00

appearances.originalFile: grail:16130 2022 H2 CJC Physics Promo Paper 1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Applies floating equilibrium and Archimedes' principle to different states.
questions.misconception: Inverting the upthrust ratio

explanation.body: When floating, the upthrust equals the block's weight, $\rho_{\mathrm{b}}Vg$, where $V$ is the block's volume. When fully submerged, the upthrust equals the weight of displaced water, $\rho_{\mathrm{w}}Vg$. Their submerged-to-floating ratio is $\frac{\rho_{\mathrm{w}}Vg}{\rho_{\mathrm{b}}Vg}=\frac{1000}{700}=1.43$.

perOption.A: Places the decimal point one place too far left in the density ratio.
perOption.B: Divides the floating upthrust by the fully submerged upthrust.
perOption.C: Correct. The ratio equals the water density divided by the wood density.
perOption.D: The densities differ by a factor of about 1.4, so a sevenfold increase is too large.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
An object of mass m is hung at one end of a 3.0 m long uniform rod of mass M and placed on a pivot. For the system to be in equilibrium, the pivot has to be placed 1.2 m from the end where the object is hung. When the object’s mass is doubled to 2m, the pivot has to be moved a distance x to the right of its original position for the system to remain in equilibrium as shown.

What is the distance x?
questions.stemText: An object of mass m is hung at one end of a 3.0 m long uniform rod of mass M and placed on a pivot. For the system to be in equilibrium, the pivot has to be placed 1.2 m from the end where the object is hung. When the object’s mass is doubled to 2m, the pivot has to be moved a distance x to the right of its original position for the system to remain in equilibrium as shown. What is the distance x? A 0.20 m B 0.40 m C 0.50 m D 0.80 m

appearances.originalFile: grail:16130 2022 H2 CJC Physics Promo Paper 1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: Balances moments twice as both lever arms change.
questions.misconception: Updating only one lever arm

explanation.body: The rod's weight acts at its centre, initially $0.30\ \mathrm{m}$ left of the pivot. Taking moments gives $(Mg)(0.30)=(mg)(1.2)$, so $M/m=4$. After moving the pivot right and doubling the hanging mass, $(Mg)(0.30+x)=(2mg)(1.2-x)$. Thus $\frac{2(1.2-x)}{0.30+x}=4$, giving $x=0.20\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The two moments balance at the new pivot.
perOption.B: Increases the rod's moment arm too far, so the rod's moment dominates.
perOption.C: Moves the pivot far enough right to give the rod a larger moment than the doubled mass.
perOption.D: Shortens the doubled mass's moment arm to 0.40 m, making its moment too small.

questions.difficultyReason: Students calculate the difference between upthrust and weight before resolving the tension.
questions.misconception: Treating upthrust as the vertical tension component

explanation.body: The downward vertical component of the tension balances upthrust minus weight, $U-W=Vg(\rho_{\mathrm{water}}-\rho_{\mathrm{buoy}})=0.500(9.81)(1000-390)\approx3000\ \mathrm{N}$. The horizontal component balances the current force $F$, so $\tan 26.6^\circ=F/3000\approx0.50$. Hence $F\approx1500\ \mathrm{N}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Uses the buoy’s weight in place of the vertical tension component and reverses the tangent ratio.
perOption.C: Divides by the tangent of the angle to the vertical.
perOption.D: Uses upthrust alone and reverses the tangent ratio.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A uniform cube of volume 0.729 $\mathrm{m}^{3}$ is floating in water. The density of water is 1000 kg $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$.

A load of 400 N is then placed onto the cube. The cube remains afloat.

What is the change in the depth of the cube submerged in the water after the load is added?
questions.stemText: A uniform cube of volume 0.729 m3 is floating in water. The density of water is 1000 kg m-3. A load of 400 N is then placed onto the cube. The cube remains afloat. What is the change in the depth of the cube submerged in the water after the load is added? A 0.0503 m B 0.0559 m C 0.494 m D 0.900 m
questions.difficultyReason: The student must get the cube’s face area from its volume and balance the added weight against the additional upthrust.
questions.misconception: Using volume in place of horizontal area

explanation.body: Let $d$ be the increase in submerged depth. The cube’s horizontal cross-sectional area is $(\sqrt[3]{0.729})^2=0.81\ \mathrm{m^2}$. By the principle of flotation, the added load equals the additional weight of displaced water, so $400=(0.81d)(1000)(9.81)$ and $d=0.0503\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Substitutes the numerical value of the cube’s volume for its cross-sectional area.
perOption.C: Divides the load by density and area without including $g$.
perOption.D: Gives the full side length of the cube.

questions.stem:
A right-angle rule hangs at rest from a peg P as shown below. The rule is uniform in density and cross-sectional area. One arm is of length L while the other arm is of length 2L.

What is the angle θ at which the rule will hang in equilibrium?
questions.stemText: A right-angle rule hangs at rest from a peg P as shown below. The rule is uniform in density and cross-sectional area. One arm is of length L while the other arm is of length 2L. L P  2L rule What is the angle θ at which the rule will hang in equilibrium? A $8^{ᵒ}$ B $14^{ᵒ}$ C $42^{ᵒ}$ D $76^{ᵒ}$
questions.difficultyReason: The student must account for unequal arm weights and resolve the perpendicular lever arms about the peg.
questions.misconception: Swapping the sine and cosine moment arms

explanation.body: If the arm of length $L$ has mass $m$, the uniform arm of length $2L$ has mass $2m$. Balance anticlockwise and clockwise moments about P using the weights at the midpoints: $(mg)(L/2)\cos\theta=(2mg)(2L/2)\sin\theta$. This gives $\tan\theta=1/4$ and $\theta=14^\circ$.

perOption.A: Gives a clockwise moment too small to balance the short arm’s anticlockwise moment.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Gives a clockwise moment larger than the short arm’s anticlockwise moment.
perOption.D: Swaps sine and cosine in the lever arms and obtains the complementary angle.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A uniform square metal sheet of length x is cut into an ‘L’ shape.

What is the distance of the centre of gravity of the sheet of metal from side AB?
questions.stemText: A uniform square metal sheet of length x is cut into an ‘L’ shape. A x B x What is the distance of the centre of gravity of the sheet of metal from side AB? A 1.0 x B 1.2 x C 1.5 x D 1.8 x
questions.difficultyReason: Locate the individual weights and equate their moments to the moment of the combined weight.
questions.misconception: Giving unequal groups equal weight

explanation.body: Let one square weigh $W$, so the two squares on the right weigh $2W$ and the whole sheet weighs $3W$. If the centre of gravity lies a horizontal distance $\bar{x}$ from B, the moment of the combined weight about B equals the sum of the individual moments: $3W\bar{x}=W(0.5x)+2W(1.5x)$. Thus $3\bar{x}=3.5x$, giving $\bar{x}=1.2x$ to two significant figures.

perOption.A: Gives equal weight to the single square and the pair when averaging their positions.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses the centre of the right-hand pair alone.
perOption.D: Places the centre of gravity beyond $1.5x$, the position of the right-hand pair’s centre.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
Several identical springs, each having the same spring constant, are joined in four arrangements. A different load is applied to each arrangement.

Which arrangement has the largest extension?
questions.stemText: Several identical springs, each having the same spring constant, are joined in four arrangements. A different load is applied to each arrangement. Which arrangement has the largest extension? A  B  C  D
questions.difficultyReason: Work out the effective spring constants in series and in parallel before comparing the four extensions.
questions.misconception: Comparing load alone

explanation.body: Let $k$ be the spring constant of one spring. For each arrangement, $F_{\mathrm{net}}=k_{\mathrm{eff}}e$, where $F_{\mathrm{net}}$ is the load and $e$ is the extension. In A, $e=2/(0.5k)=4/k$, and in B, $e=1/(k/3)=3/k$. In C, $e=6/(2k)=3/k$, and in D, $e=8/(3k)\approx2.7/k$. A has the largest extension.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: The smaller load on the three springs in series gives only $3/k$.
perOption.C: The two parallel springs share the load, giving only $3/k$.
perOption.D: The three parallel springs give the smallest extension, about $2.7/k$.

questions.stem:
A uniform sheet of metal of height 4.0 cm and width 4.0 cm has a rectangular hole, measuring 2.0 cm by 1.0 cm, cut in it as shown below.

Point M is the mid-point of the top of the sheet.

What is the distance from point M of the centre of gravity of the sheet of metal?
questions.stemText: A uniform sheet of metal of height 4.0 cm and width 4.0 cm has a rectangular hole, measuring 2.0 cm by 1.0 cm, cut in it as shown below. M 4.0 cm 0.5 cm 1.0 cm 0.5 cm 2.0 cm 1.0 cm 1.0 cm Point M is the mid-point of the top of the sheet. What is the distance from point M of the centre of gravity of the sheet of metal? A 1.7 cm B 1.9 cm C 2.1 cm D 2.3 cm
questions.difficultyReason: Requires treating the hole as negative mass and taking a weighted average of centres.
questions.misconception: Ignoring the removed area or measuring the hole position from the wrong edge

explanation.body: The complete sheet and the cut-out have centres $2.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ and $3.0\ \mathrm{cm}$ below M, respectively. Subtract the cut-out's first moment from the complete sheet's, giving $\rho tg[(4.0)(4.0)(2.0)-(1.0)(2.0)(3.0)]=26\rho tg$, using centimetres throughout. The remaining weight times its distance $y$ below M is $14\rho tg\,y$, so $y=26/14=1.857\ \mathrm{cm}\approx1.9\ \mathrm{cm}$.

perOption.A: Shifts the centre too far upward for a cut-out of area $2.0\ \mathrm{cm^2}$.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Shifts the centre toward the cut-out, as if the removed metal added weight.
perOption.D: Shifts the centre downward despite the removal of metal below the original centre.

A trailer of weight 30 kN is attached to a cab at X, as shown in the diagram.

What is the upward force exerted at X by the cab on the trailer?

questions.difficultyReason: The student must find both lever arms from the rear wheel before balancing moments.
questions.misconception: Using the interval between the forces as both lever arms.

explanation.body: Take moments about the trailer’s rear wheel. The upward force $F$ at X acts $20\ \mathrm m$ from the pivot and the weight acts $10\ \mathrm m$ from it. Balancing moments gives $F(20)=30(10)$, hence $F=15\ \mathrm{kN}$.

perOption.A: Uses an incorrect lever-arm ratio of one tenth instead of one half.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A solid metal cylinder stands on a horizontal surface, as shown.

The cylinder has length x and cross-sectional area A. The cylinder exerts a pressure p on the surface. The acceleration of free fall is g. Which expression gives the density of the metal of the cylinder?
questions.stemText: A solid metal cylinder stands on a horizontal surface, as shown. area A cylinder surface The cylinder has length x and cross-sectional area A. The cylinder exerts a pressure p on the surface. The acceleration of free fall is g. Which expression gives the density of the metal of the cylinder? A gx pA B pA gx C gx p D p gx
questions.difficultyReason: The student must link pressure to contact force and express mass in terms of density and volume.
questions.misconception: Retaining cross-sectional area after it cancels.

explanation.body: The cylinder exerts a downward force $pA$ on the surface, so by Newton’s third law the surface exerts an upward force of the same magnitude on the cylinder. In equilibrium this force equals its weight, so $pA=mg$. Substituting $m=\rho Ax$ gives $p=\rho xg$, hence $\rho=p/(gx)$.

perOption.A: Inverts the density expression and incorrectly retains the area.
perOption.B: Omits the area from the volume $Ax$ when converting mass to density.
perOption.C: Inverts the density expression.
perOption.D: Correct. The area cancels, giving $\rho=p/(gx)$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A balloon inflated with helium gas is suspended in air. The total mass of the balloon, helium and load is 80.0 kg. The density of air is about 0.00123 g $\mathrm{cm}^{-3}$.

Which of the following is the best estimate for the volume of the balloon?
questions.stemText: A balloon inflated with helium gas is suspended in air. The total mass of the balloon, helium and load is 80.0 kg. The density of air is about 0.00123 g cm-3. Which of the following is the best estimate for the volume of the balloon? A 65 $\mathrm{m}^{3}$ B 65 $\mathrm{cm}^{3}$ C 638 $\mathrm{m}^{3}$ D 638 $\mathrm{cm}^{3}$
questions.difficultyReason: Students must balance weight against buoyancy and convert the air density to consistent units.
questions.misconception: Using weight in place of mass after cancelling gravity

explanation.body: The balloon is in equilibrium, so the upthrust equals its weight, $U=mg=80.0(9.81)\ \mathrm{N}$. Using $U=V\rho_{\mathrm{air}}g$ with $\rho_{\mathrm{air}}=1.23\ \mathrm{kg\,m^{-3}}$ gives $V=65\ \mathrm{m^3}$.

perOption.A: Correct. The balloon displaces 80.0 kg of air.
perOption.B: Uses cubic centimetres for the result obtained with the density in SI units.
perOption.C: Divides the weight by the air density without the matching factor of $g$ in the upthrust.
perOption.D: Uses cubic centimetres and a value consistent with leaving an extra factor of $g$.

questions.stemText:

C 2.50
D 3.27

questions.difficultyReason: The calculation requires finding the centre of each section and converting lengths into volumes.
questions.misconception: Measuring a moment arm to the end of a section.

explanation.body:
The weights of the wood and rubber act at their midpoints, respectively $0.900L$ and $1.60L$ from the pivot. Taking moments about the pivot gives $W_{\mathrm{wood}}(0.900L)=W_{\mathrm{rubber}}(1.60L)$.

Using the common cross-sectional area $A$, the weights are $\rho_{\mathrm{wood}}(4.00L)Ag$ and $\rho_{\mathrm{rubber}}LAg$. Cancelling the common factors gives $\rho_{\mathrm{rubber}}/\rho_{\mathrm{wood}}=4.00(0.900)/1.60=2.25$.

perOption.A: Measures the rubber’s moment arm to the far end of the handle.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses an incorrect ratio of moment arms about the pivot.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A vertical tube, closed at one end, is immersed in water. A column of air is trapped inside the tube as shown.

The density of water is 1000 kg $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$.

questions.stemText: A vertical tube, closed at one end, is immersed in water. A column of air is trapped inside the tube as shown. The density of water is 1000 kg m-3. What is the difference between the pressure of the air in the tube and the atmospheric pressure? A 1960 Pa B 2940 Pa C 4910 Pa D 7850 Pa
questions.difficultyReason: The calculation is direct once the interface depth is identified.
questions.misconception: Using depth of the tube opening

explanation.body: The air–water interface is $0.50\ \mathrm{m}$ beneath the free surface. The pressure difference is $\Delta p=h\rho g=(0.50)(1000)(9.81)\approx4910\ \mathrm{Pa}$.

perOption.A: This uses the depth of the closed top of the tube.
perOption.B: This uses a single $0.30\ \mathrm{m}$ segment instead of the full interface depth.
perOption.C: Correct. The interface depth is $0.50\ \mathrm{m}$.
perOption.D: This uses the depth of the open lower end.

questions.misconception: Using the card’s width as the moment arm.

questions.stem:
A lump of ice floats in water as shown.

Which statement is correct?
questions.stemText: A lump of ice floats in water as shown. ice water Which statement is correct? A The lump of ice floats because the area of its lower surface is larger than the area of its upper surface. B The pressure difference between the lower and upper surface of the lump of ice gives rise to an upthrust equal to its weight. C The ice has a greater density than the water. D The mass of water displaced by the ice is equal to the upthrust.

options.label: A
options.text: The lump of ice floats because the area of its lower surface is larger than the area of its upper surface.

options.label: B
options.text: The pressure difference between the lower and upper surface of the lump of ice gives rise to an upthrust equal to its weight.

options.label: C
options.text: The ice has a greater density than the water.

options.label: D
options.text: The mass of water displaced by the ice is equal to the upthrust.

questions.difficultyReason: Students must connect the pressure gradient with upthrust and the force balance for floating ice.
questions.misconception: Equating upthrust to displaced mass

explanation.body: The ice floats in equilibrium, so its upthrust is $U=m_{\mathrm{ice}}g$. Water pressure increases with depth, and the pressure difference between the top and bottom gives rise to the net upward force.

perOption.A: Floating depends on the net force due to pressure, so comparing the two surface areas alone does not establish equilibrium.
perOption.B: Correct. The pressure difference produces an upthrust that balances the weight.
perOption.C: Ice floating partly submerged has a lower density than water.
perOption.D: The upthrust equals the weight of the displaced water, which is its mass multiplied by gravitational field strength.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A uniform diving board of length 5.0 m and mass 50 kg is hinged at one end and supported 2.0 m from this end by a spring of spring constant 10 kN $\mathrm{m}^{-1}$. A child of mass 40 kg stands at the far end of the board.

What is the extra compression of the spring caused by the child standing on the end of the board? (Assume the diving board remains horizontal with and without the child standing on it.)
questions.stemText: A uniform diving board of length 5.0 m and mass 50 kg is hinged at one end and supported 2.0 m from this end by a spring of spring constant 10 kN m−1. A child of mass 40 kg stands at the far end of the board. What is the extra compression of the spring caused by the child standing on the end of the board? (Assume the diving board remains horizontal with and without the child standing on it.) A 1.0 cm B 6.1 cm C 9.8 cm D 16 cm
questions.difficultyReason: Students must combine moment balance with Hooke's law and isolate the change in spring compression.
questions.misconception: Reporting total compression instead of extra compression

explanation.body: Balance clockwise and anticlockwise moments about the hinge. For compression $x$ without the child, $(10000x)(2.0)=(50\times9.81)(2.5)$. For compression $x'$ with the child, $(10000x')(2.0)=(40\times9.81)(5.0)+(50\times9.81)(2.5)$. Subtracting gives $x'-x=0.0981\ \mathrm{m}$, or $9.8\ \mathrm{cm}$.

perOption.A: This is consistent with a factor-of-ten error converting $0.0981\ \mathrm{m}$ to centimetres.
perOption.B: This is the compression due to the board alone.
perOption.C: Correct. Subtracting the moment equations isolates the extra compression.
perOption.D: This is the total compression with the child, including the board's contribution.

questions.stemText: A sledge slides down a slope at a constant velocity. The three forces that act on the sledge are the normal contact force C, the weight W and a constant frictional force F. Which diagram represents these forces acting on the sledge? A  B  C  D
questions.difficultyReason: Students must match the directions of the forces and check that the vector triangle closes.
questions.misconception: Assuming every triangular arrangement of arrows represents zero net force

explanation.body: The sledge moves at constant velocity, so its net force is zero. Its three force vectors must therefore form a closed triangle when placed head to tail.

perOption.A: Friction points down the slope and the arrows do not close head to tail.
perOption.B: The weight arrow points up instead of vertically down.
perOption.C: Correct. The arrows close head to tail with weight pointing down.
perOption.D: The contact force points into the slope and the arrows do not close head to tail.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
A submarine is in equilibrium in a fully submerged position as shown.

[Cross-section of a submerged submarine with a steel hull surrounding air and sea water outside.]

What causes the upthrust on the submarine?

A The air in the submarine is less dense than sea water.
B The submarine displaces its own volume of sea water.
C The sea water exerts a greater upward force on the submarine than the weight of the submarine.
D There is a difference in water pressure acting on the top and on the bottom of the submarine.

stemImage.alt: Question 9: A submarine is in equilibrium in a fully submerged position as shown. What causes the upthrust on the submarine?

questions.difficultyReason: Recall how increasing fluid pressure with depth produces upthrust.
questions.misconception: Confusing the magnitude of upthrust with its physical origin

explanation.body: Water pressure increases with depth, so it is greater at the bottom of the submarine than at the top. The resulting net upward pressure force is the upthrust.

perOption.A: The air density affects the submarine’s average density, while the upthrust comes from the surrounding water pressure.
perOption.B: Displaced volume determines the upthrust’s magnitude, while the pressure difference produces it.
perOption.C: In equilibrium the net upward force from the water equals the submarine’s weight.
perOption.D: Correct. Pressure is greater at the bottom than at the top.

questions.stemText:
A hinged trapdoor is held closed in the horizontal position by a cable that is connected midway between the hinge and the centre of gravity of the trapdoor.

[The trapdoor extends horizontally from a hinge on a vertical wall. Cable tension $T$ points up and left along the cable towards the wall. The hinge force $H$ points down and right from the hinge. Weight $W$ points vertically down at the centre of gravity.]

(forces are not drawn to scale)

Three forces act on the trapdoor: the weight $W$ of the trapdoor, the tension $T$ in the cable and the force $H$ at the hinge.

Which list gives the three forces in increasing order of magnitude?

A $H, W, T$
B $H, T, W$
C $W, H, T$
D $W, T, H$

stemImage.alt: Question 10: A hinged trapdoor is held closed in the horizontal position by a cable that is connected midway between the hinge and the centre of gravity of the trapdoor. (fo

questions.difficultyReason: Combine force balance in two directions with a moment balance about the cable attachment.
questions.misconception: Comparing force magnitudes without resolving components

explanation.body: Vertical equilibrium gives $T\sin\phi=H\sin\theta+W$, with both angles measured from horizontal. The horizontal components balance, so the larger vertical component gives $T>H$, and the vertical equation also gives $T>W$. Taking moments about the cable attachment gives $(L/4)H\sin\theta=(L/4)W$. Thus $H>W$, giving $W<H<T$.

perOption.A: The hinge’s downward component equals the weight, so the full hinge force is greater than the weight.
perOption.B: The tension’s vertical component alone exceeds the weight.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
The spring system shown is composed of two springs, P and Q, of negligible mass connected in series. P has a spring constant of $30\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$ and Q has a spring constant of $10\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$.

[Spring P hangs from a fixed support, spring Q hangs below P, and a $3.0\ \mathrm{N}$ load hangs from Q.]

When a $3.0\ \mathrm{N}$ load is supported by the system, which of the following is the overall extension produced?

A $40\ \mathrm{mm}$
B $150\ \mathrm{mm}$
C $400\ \mathrm{mm}$
D $433\ \mathrm{mm}$

stemImage.alt: Question 7: The spring system shown is composed of two springs, P and Q, of negligible mass connected in series. P has a spring constant of 30 N m1 and Q has a spring cons

questions.difficultyReason: Apply Hooke’s law to each spring and add the extensions.
questions.misconception: Treating series springs as sharing the load.

explanation.body: Both springs carry the same tension of $3.0\ \mathrm{N}$. Their extensions are $x_P=3/30=0.10\ \mathrm{m}$ and $x_Q=3/10=0.30\ \mathrm{m}$. perOption.A: Gives an extension ten times too small, as with a misplaced decimal in the unit conversion.

explanation.body: The two equal weights combine into a downward force $2W$ acting midway between their lines of action. In equilibrium the three nonparallel forces must have a common point of intersection. The line of action of $2W$ meets the wire at D, so the hinge force acts along AD.

The density of X is less than that of Y. The rod is horizontal when suspended from a string attached at the centre of the rod. P Q Y X Which object has the smaller mass? The cross-sectional area of each cylinder is 12.5 $\mathrm{m}^{2}$.

How much does the platform rise in the lake when the vehicle is removed from it?

Four hollow metal cylinders of equal volume are installed vertically below the four corners of the floating platform as shown. floating platform lake surface hollow metal cylinder The cross-sectional area of each cylinder is 12.5 m2. questions.difficultyReason: It requires equating the change in upthrust to the removed weight and relating displaced volume to all four cylinders.
questions.misconception: Using the cross-sectional area of just one cylinder.

explanation.body: At equilibrium, the extra upthrust $U$ balances the vehicle’s weight $W$, giving $W=U$ and $mg=\rho Vg$. For a rise $h$, the change in displaced volume is $4\times12.5\times h$, so $2.0\times10^4=(4\times12.5\times h)\times1000$. This gives $h=0.40\ \mathrm{m}$.

perOption.A: Uses the cross-sectional area of only one cylinder.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: Uses twice the actual total cross-sectional area.
perOption.D: Divides by four again after already accounting for the four cylinders.

questions.difficultyReason: Students must read the moment arms and distinguish the change in reaction from the final reaction.

explanation.body: Take moments about the rear axle. Before loading, $Wx=N(2x)$, so the front-axle reaction is $N=\frac W2$. With the block loaded, $Wx+w(3x)=N'(2x)$, so $N'=\frac{W+3w}{2}$. The reaction therefore increases by $N'-N=\frac{3w}{2}$.

B $\frac{Ty}{x}$

D $\frac{T(y-L)}{x-L}$

appearances.originalFile: grail:12822 EJC 2023 J1 H2 Promo P1 QP

questions.difficultyReason: The main step is identifying extension as the stretched length minus the natural length.
questions.misconception: Using total length in Hooke’s law.

explanation.body: By Hooke’s law, tension is directly proportional to extension. The extensions are $x-L$ under tension $T$ and $y-L$ under tension $T'$. Therefore $\frac{T'}{T}=\frac{y-L}{x-L}$, giving $T'=\frac{T(y-L)}{x-L}$.

perOption.A: Uses total lengths and makes tension decrease as the wire length increases.
perOption.B: Uses a direct ratio of total lengths instead of extensions.

questions.difficultyReason: The calculation requires subtracting the block’s weight from the upthrust before applying Newton’s second law.

explanation.body: Taking upwards as positive, Newton’s second law gives $U-m_{\mathrm{wood}}g-T=m_{\mathrm{wood}}a$. questions.stem: A rigid body is acted upon by a number of coplanar forces. Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.stemText: A rigid body is acted upon by a number of coplanar forces. Which of the following statements is correct? A When the vector sum of all the forces acting on the body is zero, the object must be in a state of static equilibrium. B When the coplanar forces are a couple, the magnitude of the torque of the couple on the object does not depend on the choice of the pivot point. C When acted upon by three non-parallel coplanar forces whose lines of action intersect at a single point, the body must be in static equilibrium. D When acted upon by two forces of equal magnitude and opposite directions, the body will always experience a net turning effect.

options.label: A
options.text: When the vector sum of all the forces acting on the body is zero, the object must be in a state of static equilibrium.

options.label: B
options.text: When the coplanar forces are a couple, the magnitude of the torque of the couple on the object does not depend on the choice of the pivot point.

options.label: C
options.text: When acted upon by three non-parallel coplanar forces whose lines of action intersect at a single point, the body must be in static equilibrium.

options.label: D
options.text: When acted upon by two forces of equal magnitude and opposite directions, the body will always experience a net turning effect.

questions.difficultyReason: Tests precise conditions for equilibrium and properties of a couple.
questions.misconception: Believing zero resultant force alone guarantees equilibrium

explanation.body: A couple consists of two equal and opposite forces and produces a pure turning effect. When their moments are added, the terms that depend on the pivot cancel, leaving a torque that is independent of the pivot.

perOption.A: Zero resultant force still allows a nonzero resultant torque.
perOption.B: Correct.
perOption.C: The forces have zero total moment about their intersection, but their resultant force can be nonzero.
perOption.D: If the forces share a line of action, their net torque is zero.

appearances.originalFile: RI/H2/2026 RI H2Phy Prelims P1 Questions.pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Students must apply the three-forces-concurrent condition and account for friction at both contact surfaces.
questions.misconception: Assuming the wall force is purely horizontal (normal only) even on a rough wall

explanation.body:
When the beam is in equilibrium under three forces ($W$, $X$ and $Y$), their lines of action must meet at a common point, so that there is no resultant moment about any point on the beam.

$W$ acts vertically down through the middle of the beam. $X$ (from the ground) and $Y$ (from the wall) each combine a normal force with friction, so both slope upward, and their lines pass through the point where $W$'s line of action crosses them. Only diagram D shows this.

perOption.A: $Y$ points down along the beam and $X$ is horizontal, so there is no upward force to balance $W$ and the forces cannot be in equilibrium.
perOption.B: $X$ points away from the wall, so nothing balances the horizontal push of $Y$, and the three lines of action do not meet at one point.
perOption.C: $Y$ is drawn horizontal, which ignores friction at the rough wall, and the three lines of action do not meet at a common point.
perOption.D: Correct. The lines of action of $X$, $Y$ and $W$ meet at one point.

The lower spring has a spring constant of $10\ \mathrm{N\,m^{-1}}$.

Both masses are in equilibrium, and both springs obey Hooke's law.

[The upper spring connects the ceiling to the first mass. The lower spring connects the first mass to the second. The diagram is not drawn to scale.]

What is the extension of the lower spring from its unstretched length?

A. $1.0\ \mathrm{cm}$
B. $1.3\ \mathrm{cm}$

questions.misconception: Assuming identical tension in both springs

explanation.body: By Hooke's law, $x=F/k$. If each mass has weight $W$, the upper spring supports both masses and has extension $x_\mathrm{upper}=2W/30$, while the lower supports one mass and has extension $x_\mathrm{lower}=W/10$. Their extension ratio is $x_\mathrm{upper}/x_\mathrm{lower}=2/3$, so $2.0/x_\mathrm{lower}=2/3$ and the lower spring extends $3.0\ \mathrm{cm}$.

Two objects P and Q having the same volume are hung at either ends of a light uniform rod and subsequently submerged in two different liquids X and Y respectively. The density of liquid X is greater than that of liquid Y. The system is balanced when a string is hung right at the centre of the rod as shown in the figure below.

Which of the following statements is correct?

The density of liquid X is greater than that of liquid Y. The system is balanced when a string is hung right at the centre of the rod as shown in the figure below. Q P liquid X liquid Y Which of the following statements is correct? A P and Q experience the same magnitudes of upthrust. B Upthrust acting on P is smaller than the upthrust acting on Q. C Mass of P is smaller than mass of Q. D Mass of P is greater than mass of Q.

options.label: A
options.text: P and Q experience the same magnitudes of upthrust.

options.label: B
options.text: Upthrust acting on P is smaller than the upthrust acting on Q.

options.label: C
options.text: Mass of P is smaller than mass of Q.

options.label: D
options.text: Mass of P is greater than mass of Q.

questions.difficultyReason: Requires combining moment balance with upthrust.
questions.misconception: Thinking equal moments imply equal weights

explanation.body:
For each mass, tension + upthrust = weight, so tension = weight $-$ upthrust.

The rod is horizontal and pivoted at its centre, so the tensions are equal.

Upthrust $=V\rho g$ is greater for P because liquid X is denser, so P's weight must be greater to give the same tension as Q.

perOption.A: Same volume but different liquid densities give different upthrusts.
perOption.B: P is in the denser liquid so its upthrust is larger, not smaller.
perOption.C: Reverses the conclusion: P needs the larger weight.
perOption.D: Correct. Larger upthrust on P means P must be heavier.

Three cuboids with identical dimensions are fully immersed in water as shown. The cuboids are held by strings in identical orientations by strings and in equilibrium at the same depth.

Water has density ρ. Cuboid W is made of material of density 4ρ. Cuboid X is made of material of density 2 ρ. Cuboid Y is made of material of density 1.5 ρ.

Which statement is correct?
questions.stemText: Three cuboids with identical dimensions are fully immersed in water as shown. The cuboids are held by strings in identical orientations by strings and in equilibrium at the same depth. 1.5 Water has density ρ. Cuboid W is made of material of density 4ρ. Cuboid X is made of material of density 2 ρ. Cuboid Y is made of material of density 1.5 ρ. Which statement is correct? A The upthrust on cuboid Y is equal to weight of cuboid Y. B The upthrust on cuboid W is two times the upthrust on cuboid X. C The tension of strings on each cuboid is the same D The tension of string on cuboid W is the greatest.

options.label: A
options.text: The upthrust on cuboid Y is equal to weight of cuboid Y.

options.label: B
options.text: The upthrust on cuboid W is two times the upthrust on cuboid X.

options.label: C
options.text: The tension of strings on each cuboid is the same

options.label: D
options.text: The tension of string on cuboid W is the greatest.

questions.difficultyReason: Upthrust depends only on displaced volume; straightforward equilibrium argument.
questions.misconception: Thinking upthrust depends on the density of the object

explanation.body:
The cuboids have equal volume and are fully immersed, so the upthrust $U$ is the same on each.

$T + U = mg = \rho_{\text{material}} V g$, so $T = \rho_{\text{material}}Vg - U$.

Cuboid W has the largest density, so the tension in its string is the greatest.

perOption.A: Y is denser than water, so its weight exceeds the upthrust (the string supplies the difference).
perOption.B: Upthrust is the same for all three because volume displaced is equal.
perOption.C: Tensions differ because the weights differ.
perOption.D: Correct. $T=\rho Vg-U$ is largest for the densest cuboid.

questions.misconception: assuming every force contributes a torque

explanation.body:
Two pairs of the forces are antiparallel and separated by a perpendicular distance $d$, forming two couples, each of torque $Fd$.

Total torque $= Fd + Fd = 2Fd$.

The other forces act along lines through the centre, so they produce no torque.

perOption.A: Counts only one of the two couples.
perOption.B: Correct. Two couples of $Fd$ each.
perOption.C: Counts an extra couple; forces whose lines of action pass through the centre give no torque.
perOption.D: Treats all eight forces as producing torque, but four act through the centre.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
An oil-drum floats in equilibrium in seawater as shown. The drum has a cross-sectional area of 0.19 $\mathrm{m}^{2}$. The length of the drum submerged under water is 0.80 m. The density of seawater is 1.1 × $10^{3}$ kg $\mathrm{m}^{-3}$.

What is the mass of the drum and its content?
questions.stemText: An oil-drum floats in equilibrium in seawater as shown. The drum has a cross-sectional area of 0.19 m2. The length of the drum submerged under water is 0.80 m. The density of seawater is 1.1 × 103 kg m−3. cross sectional area 0.19 m2 drum 0.80 m seawater What is the mass of the drum and its content? A 167 kg B 251 kg C 1640 kg D 1770 kg
questions.difficultyReason: Direct application of upthrust equals weight for a floating body.
questions.misconception: confusing weight in N with mass in kg

explanation.body:
Atmospheric pressure acts on both the top and bottom of the drum, so its effect cancels.

At equilibrium, weight of drum and content = weight of water displaced $= V\rho g = 0.80\times0.19\times1.1\times10^{3}\times9.81 = 1640\ \mathrm{N}$.

Mass of drum and content $= \dfrac{1640}{9.81} = 167\ \mathrm{kg}$.

perOption.A: Correct. $m = \rho V = 1.1\times10^3 \times 0.80 \times 0.19 = 167\ \mathrm{kg}$.
perOption.B: Does not follow from the displaced volume and the seawater density.
perOption.C: This is the weight in newtons, not the mass in kilograms.
perOption.D: Does not follow from the displaced volume; the upthrust equals the weight, so the mass is $\rho V$.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A rod YW is first balanced on a pivot placed at 1.05 m from the end Y.

A 200 g mass is now tied to the rod by a light string at a distance of 0.10 m from point Y. In order to balance the rod horizontally, the rod is now pivoted at a new position that is 0.27 m
questions.stemText: A rod YW is first balanced on a pivot placed at 1.05 m from the end Y. pivot Y W 1.05 m A 200 g mass is now tied to the rod by a light string at a distance of 0.10 m from point Y. In order to balance the rod horizontally, the rod is now pivoted at a new position that is 0.27 m to the left of the original position. W Y 0.10 m 0.27 m 200 g What is the mass of the rod? A 500 g B 580 g C 700 g D 830 g
questions.difficultyReason: Students must locate the rod’s centre of gravity and calculate both lever arms about the shifted pivot.
questions.misconception: The rod’s own centre of gravity shifts when the suspended mass is added.

explanation.body: The rod’s original balance point is its centre of gravity. After the mass is attached, the new pivot is $0.27\ \mathrm{m}$ to its left and the suspended mass is $1.05-0.10-0.27=0.68\ \mathrm{m}$ from the new pivot. Taking moments about the new pivot gives $mg(0.27)=0.200g(0.68)$, so $m=0.503\ \mathrm{kg}$, approximately $500\ \mathrm{g}$.

perOption.A: Correct.
perOption.B: Requires too large a lever arm for the suspended mass about the new pivot.
perOption.C: Uses the approximately $0.95\ \mathrm{m}$ distance from the mass to the original pivot.
perOption.D: Would require a lever arm greater than $1.05\ \mathrm{m}$ for the suspended mass, even though the new pivot lies only $0.78\ \mathrm{m}$ from Y.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
The diagrams show a hollow metal cube, with a sealed opening, is suspended from a spring balance before and during immersion in water. A reduction in the balance reading occurs because of the immersion.

Water is then allowed to enter the metal cube, through the opening, to fill up the empty space in the cube. Which of the following statements is correct?
questions.stemText: The diagrams show a hollow metal cube, with a sealed opening, is suspended from a spring balance before and during immersion in water. A reduction in the balance reading occurs because of the immersion. Water is then allowed to enter the metal cube, through the opening, to fill up the empty space in the cube. Which of the following statements is correct? A Upthrust of the water on the cube increases, hence the balance reading will be further reduced. B The balance reading during immersion corresponds to the upthrust of the water on the cube. C The balance reading stays the same as the increase in weight of water in the cube is offset by the increase in upthrust of the water on the cube. D The balance reading increases due to the increase of gravitational pull on the cube.

options.label: A
options.text: Upthrust of the water on the cube increases, hence the balance reading will be further reduced.

options.label: B
options.text: The balance reading during immersion corresponds to the upthrust of the water on the cube.

options.label: C
options.text: The balance reading stays the same as the increase in weight of water in the cube is offset by the increase in upthrust of the water on the cube.

options.label: D
options.text: The balance reading increases due to the increase of gravitational pull on the cube.

questions.difficultyReason: Needs the idea that upthrust depends only on the displaced volume, not on what is inside the cube.
questions.misconception: Water entering the cube increases the upthrust

explanation.body:
Upthrust equals the weight of water displaced by the cube. The cube's external volume does not change, so the upthrust does not change.

For the cube in equilibrium, tension + upthrust = weight, so the balance reading (tension) = weight − upthrust; it is not the upthrust itself.

As water fills the empty space, the weight of the cube (with its contents) increases while the upthrust stays the same, so the balance reading increases.

perOption.A: Upthrust depends on the volume displaced, which is unchanged, so upthrust does not increase.
perOption.B: The reading is the tension, equal to weight − upthrust, not the upthrust.
perOption.C: Upthrust does not change, so the extra weight of water is not offset and the reading rises.
perOption.D: Correct. The weight increases while the upthrust is unchanged.

questions.stem: Which person in the following situations is experiencing weightlessness?
questions.stemText: Which person in the following situations is experiencing weightlessness? A An athlete clearing the bar in a high jump. B A swimmer floating in water. C A parachutist falling at terminal speed. D A pilot in a hovering helicopter.

options.label: A
options.text: An athlete clearing the bar in a high jump.

options.label: C
options.text: A parachutist falling at terminal speed.

options.label: D
options.text: A pilot in a hovering helicopter.

questions.difficultyReason: The student distinguishes free fall from situations where a contact force supports the person.
questions.misconception: Equating zero acceleration with weightlessness.

explanation.body: A person feels weightless in free fall when gravity alone acts on them. While the athlete clears the bar, gravity is the only appreciable force.

perOption.A: Correct. The athlete is in free fall.
perOption.B: The water exerts an upward buoyant force.
perOption.C: The parachute harness exerts an upward force on the parachutist.
perOption.D: The seat exerts an upward normal force on the pilot.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem: Which of the following statements is true?
questions.stemText: Which of the following statements is true? A When a moving object experiences friction, the work done against friction is independent of the path taken by the object. B An object which experiences a resistive force always reaches terminal speed. C Friction always hinders motion. D There are certain situations in which friction does not cause energy to be lost to the surroundings.

options.label: A
options.text: When a moving object experiences friction, the work done against friction is independent of the path taken by the object.

options.label: B
options.text: An object which experiences a resistive force always reaches terminal speed.

options.label: D
options.text: There are certain situations in which friction does not cause energy to be lost to the surroundings.

questions.difficultyReason: A stationary object under static friction supplies a counterexample to the claim that friction always dissipates energy.
questions.misconception: Assuming all friction dissipates energy.

explanation.body: If you push an object and static friction balances your push, the object stays still. With zero displacement, the work done against friction and the energy dissipated are both zero.

perOption.A: Work done against friction depends on the path taken.
perOption.B: A falling object can hit the ground before reaching terminal speed.
perOption.C: Friction between our feet and the ground allows us to move forward.
perOption.D: Correct. Static friction can act while the object stays still.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stem:
A horizontal bar is supported on a pivot at its centre of gravity. A fixed load is attached to one end of the bar. To keep the bar in equilibrium, a force F is applied at a distance x from the pivot.

How does F vary with x?
questions.stemText: A horizontal bar is supported on a pivot at its centre of gravity. A fixed load is attached to one end of the bar. To keep the bar in equilibrium, a force F is applied at a distance x from the pivot. How does F vary with x? A  B  C  D

appearances.originalFile: grail:10487 YIJC 2023 H2Phy Prelim P1 Question Paper

questions.difficultyReason: A direct application of the principle of moments followed by recognising an inverse-proportion graph.

explanation.body:
The load (weight $W$) is constant and the pivot is fixed, a distance $h$ from the load.

Taking moments about the pivot: $Wh = Fx$.

$Wh$ is constant since $W$ and $h$ are constant, so $Fx$ = constant and $F \propto 1/x$. Graph B shows this relationship.

perOption.A: A straight line with negative gradient would mean $F$ decreases linearly, not $F \propto 1/x$.
perOption.B: Correct. $Fx$ is constant, an inverse-proportion curve.
perOption.C: $F$ decreases, not increases, as its moment arm $x$ grows.
perOption.D: $F$ must fall as $x$ increases, since a larger arm needs a smaller force for the same moment.

questions.stemText: A cylinder of weight W is placed on a smooth slope. The contact force of the slope on the cylinder is R. A thread is attached to the surface of the cylinder. The other end of the thread is fixed. Which diagram shows the cylinder in equilibrium? A  B  C  D

appearances.originalFile: grail:10487 YIJC 2023 H2Phy Prelim P1 Question Paper

questions.difficultyReason: Requires knowing the concurrency condition for three forces and checking it carefully on diagrams.
questions.misconception: Thinking that balanced force magnitudes alone guarantee equilibrium, ignoring torque

explanation.body:
The cylinder is in equilibrium under three forces: $R$, $W$ and the tension in the thread.

For a body in equilibrium under three non-parallel forces, their lines of action must pass through a common point. Only in option C do all three lines meet at one point.

perOption.A: The lines of action of the three forces do not meet at a single point, so there is a resultant torque.
perOption.B: The thread's line of action does not pass through the point where $R$ and $W$ meet.
perOption.C: Correct. $R$, $W$ and the tension are concurrent.
perOption.D: The three lines of action do not pass through a common point.

A horizontal beam has its centre of gravity at X. It is supported by a vertical wire attached to the beam at point R as indicated on the diagram. The tension in the wire is equal to the weight of the beam.
[Diagram: horizontal beam between two hatched walls with sockets P (left) and Q (right). Point R is near the left end, with an upward arrow labelled 'tension'. X, the centre of gravity, is to the right of R, near the middle of the beam, with a downward arrow labelled 'weight'.]
The ends of the beam fit into the sockets P and Q in two rigid vertical walls which keep the beam in equilibrium.
What are the directions of the forces acting on the beam at sockets P and Q?
| | socket P | socket Q |
| A | upwards | upwards |
| B | upwards | downwards |
| C | downwards | upwards |
| D | downwards | downwards |

questions.difficultyReason: Requires choosing pivots and comparing moment arms rather than just balancing vertical forces.
questions.misconception: Assuming supports always push upwards

explanation.body:
Take moments about P: the weight acts further from P than the tension (which equals it), so the weight's clockwise moment is larger. The force at Q must be upwards to balance it.

Take moments about Q: the tension acts further from Q than the weight, giving a larger (clockwise about Q) moment from the tension. The force at P must be downwards to balance it.

perOption.A: If both sockets pushed up, the total upward force would exceed the weight, since tension already equals weight.
perOption.B: Reverses both directions; moments about P show Q must push up, not down.
perOption.C: Correct. Moments about P and about Q fix Q upwards and P downwards.
perOption.D: Two downward socket forces cannot balance moments about P, where the weight's moment exceeds the tension's.

questions.subject: h2-physics
questions.stemText:
Four combinations of vectors are shown, each representing all the forces acting on an object. The forces all act in the same plane.

The object is in equilibrium.

Which combination of vectors could represent the forces acting on the object?

[A: A vertical downward vector forms the left side of a triangle. The vectors from its top and bottom both point towards the right vertex.
B: A vertical downward vector and a down-left diagonal both end at a corner from which a horizontal rightward vector starts.
C: A diagonal vector points down-left into a junction. Two vectors leave the junction, one pointing steeply down-left and one pointing down-right.
D: An upward vertical vector and a down-right diagonal start at the same point. A down-left diagonal starts at the tip of the down-right vector and ends directly below the start of the upward vector.]

stemImage.alt: Question 2: Four combinations of vectors are shown, each representing all the forces acting on an object. The forces all act in the same plane. The object is in equilibrium

appearances.originalFile: YIJC/2026 JC2 H2 Prelim Paper 1 QP (Revised).pdf

questions.difficultyReason: Rearrange the vectors tip to tail while preserving their directions to check for zero resultant.
questions.misconception: Taking any triangular arrangement to mean zero vector sum.

explanation.body: Rearrange each set of force vectors tip to tail without changing their directions or lengths. Only D gives a closed vector triangle and hence zero resultant force, as required for equilibrium. A, B and C all give a nonzero resultant.

perOption.A: Both diagonal vectors have rightward components, so the horizontal forces cannot cancel.
perOption.B: The vertical and diagonal vectors both have downward components, with no upward component to balance them.
perOption.C: All three vectors have downward components, so the vertical forces cannot cancel.
perOption.D: Correct. The three vectors form a closed triangle when arranged tip to tail.
